title: Hall Sloppy Joe Feed
seoTitle: Hall Sloppy Joe Feed | Firefighter Meal
shortDescription: Sweet-tangy beef sloppy joes with buns and chips for ten
subtitle: Sweet-tangy beef sloppy joes with buns and chips for ten
description: Ground beef browns with onion and bell pepper, then simmers in a sweet-tangy tomato sauce until thick and scoopable. Pile on toasted buns with pickles and chips for a classic hall feed.

steps.title: Gather ingredients and equipment
steps.instruction: Line up every ingredient for Hall Sloppy Joe Feed in the order you will cook — measure spices into ramekins, trim proteins on a dedicated board, and set tongs, thermometers, and hotel pans within arm's reach before any heat goes on.

steps.title: Preheat ovens and surfaces
steps.instruction: Preheat ovens, griddles, or grills to recipe temp before the crew arrives — cold equipment extends cook time and dries out batch beef. Confirm burners ignite evenly and sheet pans are greased or lined.

steps.title: Brown the beef
steps.instruction: Cook ground beef with onion and bell pepper over medium-high heat 12–15 minutes, breaking into crumbles until well browned. Drain excess fat.

steps.title: Build the sauce
steps.instruction: Stir in ketchup, tomato paste, Worcestershire, vinegar, and brown sugar until combined. Plan about 3 minutes for this step at crew scale. Work in batches if the pan or grill crowding steams food instead of browning — rookies should watch for pale surfaces and adjust heat early.

steps.title: Simmer until thick
steps.instruction: Reduce heat and simmer uncovered 15–20 minutes, stirring often, until sauce mounds on a spoon and flavors meld. Maintain a steady simmer — bubbles should break the surface without a rolling boil that shreds delicate proteins. Work in batches if the pan or grill crowding steams food instead of browning — rookies should watch for pale surfaces and adjust heat early.

steps.title: Toast the buns
steps.instruction: Split buns and toast cut-side down in a dry skillet or under broiler at 400°F until golden, about 3 minutes. Target oven/smoker temperature: 400°F.

steps.title: Verify safe internal temps
steps.instruction: Spot-check the thickest pieces with an instant-read thermometer — target 145°F for medium beef, 160°F for ground. If any piece reads low, return it to heat immediately rather than holding under temp on the line.

steps.title: Hold for call interruptions
steps.instruction: If tones drop mid-service, cover finished food and hold at 140°F in a warm cabinet or 200°F oven — never leave proteins below 140°F for more than 30 minutes cumulative. Note the hold time on the pan with a grease pencil.

steps.title: Portion and open the line
steps.instruction: Portion Hall Sloppy Joe Feed onto sheet trays or hotel pans for family-style service. Stack plates, forks, and napkins at the end of the line so late-arriving crew can self-serve without bottlenecking the cook.

steps.title: Scale for larger halls
steps.instruction: When cooking for more than 10 firefighters, split into two pans halfway through so the bottom layer does not overcook while the top waits — duplicate mise en place if you double batches.

steps.title: Serve the line
steps.instruction: Hold beef warm at 165°F in a hotel pan. Crews build sandwiches with pickles and extra onion if desired. Serve with chips. Plan about 5 minutes for this step at crew scale. Work in batches if the pan or grill crowding steams food instead of browning — rookies should watch for pale surfaces and adjust heat early.

proTips: A tablespoon of mustard adds tang without making it taste like mustard.
Smoked paprika pinch makes canned-sauce flavors taste more homemade.
Coleslaw on the sandwich is messy but worth it if you have time.
tonightSpread: Sloppy joes with kettle chips and dill pickles.
Baked beans from a can, doctored with molasses and mustard, for a cookout vibe.
leftovers: Serve over baked potatoes with shredded cheese.
Fold into a casserole with tater tots and cheddar for sloppy joe hot dish.
whyCrewsLikeIt: Sloppy joes are cheap, fast, and universally loved—especially by crews who grew up on cafeteria versions. This recipe is thicker and meatier, built for ten hungry firefighters.
mealPrepNotes: Brown beef hard and drain fat or sandwiches get greasy. Sauce should mound on a spoon, not run off the bun. Toast buns so they survive the saucy filling.
